## Data Source and Description

```
**Dataset:** Hotel Booking Demand

**Description:** Booking records from two hotels in Portugal, a resort hotel
in the Algarve and a city hotel in Lisbon, for arrivals between July 1, 2015
and August 31, 2017. Each row is one booking. The file has 119,390 rows and 
32 columns, with details such as lead time, length of stay, number of guests,
market segment, deposit type and average daily rate. The target variable is
`is_canceled` (1 = the booking was canceled, 0 = it was not).

**Progject Goal:** Using only what is known when a booking is made, can we predict whether the guest will fail to stay, either by cancelling or by not showing up?

**Original source:** Antonio, N., de Almeida, A., & Nunes, L. (2019). Hotel
booking demand datasets. *Data in Brief, 22*, 41–49.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dib.2018.11.126

**Obtained from:** TidyTuesday (R for Data Science community), release of
February 11, 2020.
https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/master/data/2020/2020-02-11
Accessed November 13, 2026.

**How this copy was prepared:** TidyTuesday combined the article's two hotel
files into one, standardized the column names and added the `hotel` column.
Our own cleaning steps are documented in the sections below.
```

## Step 2. Defining question & remove leakage

At the moment a booking is made, can we predict whether it will be cancelled?
The two parts of it:  “At the moment a booking is made” sets the time of the prediction. It is the reason the columns filled in later have to be removed: the final status, its date, the assigned room and the count of booking changes. “Whether it will be cancelled” is the target, "is_canceled."

```{r}
table(hotels$reservation_status, hotels$is_canceled)
```
The 44,224 are 43,017 cancellations plus 1,207 no-shows, so the target means “did not stay”

```{r}
hotels_clean <- subset(hotels, select = -c(reservation_status,
                                           reservation_status_date,
                                           assigned_room_type,
                                           booking_changes,
                                           required_car_parking_spaces))
dim(hotels_clean)
```
### Leakage columns removed

| Column                    | What it holds                              | Why it leaks                                      |
|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| `reservation_status`      | Final status: Canceled, Check-Out, No-Show | It is the outcome under another name              |
| `reservation_status_date` | Date the final status was set              | Exists only after the outcome has happened        |
| `assigned_room_type`      | Room type actually given to the guest      | Set at or near check-in, after the booking is made |
| `booking_changes`         | Changes/amendments made to the booking     | Counts changes made after booking; not known at the time of booking |
|`required_car_parking_spaces`| Requested Parking Spaces.                | Determined at check-in                            |



```{r}
table(hotels$deposit_type, hotels$reservation_status)
```

## Test 1: are no-deposit bookings made at the last minute?
```{r}
tapply(hotels$lead_time, hotels$deposit_type, summary)
```
## Test 2: are non-refundable bookings made online?
```{r}
table(hotels$deposit_type, hotels$market_segment)
```



## Step 3a:  Count missing items: 

The first counts true missing values in each column, and the second counts cells holding the text "NULL".

```{r}
colSums(is.na(hotels_clean))
colSums(hotels_clean == "NULL", na.rm = TRUE)
```
## Step 3b: Fix the missing values
```{r}
length(unique(hotels_clean$agent))
length(unique(hotels_clean$company))
```
This counts the distinct values in each column. Found: 334 and 353 distinct values. Neither model can make good use of a category with hundreds of levels: k-NN would need hundreds of extra columns, and naive Bayes would have very few bookings per code to learn from..

## The Fix
```{r}
# 1. children: replace the 4 missing values with 0
hotels_clean$children[is.na(hotels_clean$children)] <- 0

# 2. country: label the unknowns
hotels_clean$country[hotels_clean$country == "NULL"] <- "Unknown"

# 3. agent and company: turn into yes/no flags, then drop the originals
hotels_clean$used_agent   <- ifelse(hotels_clean$agent == "NULL", 0, 1)
hotels_clean$used_company <- ifelse(hotels_clean$company == "NULL", 0, 1)
hotels_clean <- subset(hotels_clean, select = -c(agent, company))
```
The reasoning for each
**children set to 0.** Only 4 rows are affected, and the great majority of bookings have no children, so 0 is the most likely true value. Keeping the rows is better than losing four bookings over one blank.
**country labeled “Unknown”. **The origin was not recorded for 488 bookings. A clear label keeps those rows and is honest about what you don’t know. Whether to use country as a predictor at all is a Step 4 question.
**agent and company become flags. **The useful information is whether an agent or a company was involved, not which one out of hundreds. ifelse() writes 0 where the value was “NULL” and 1 otherwise. Once the flags exist, the original columns are dropped.

```{r}
colSums(is.na(hotels_clean))
table(hotels_clean$used_agent)
table(hotels_clean$used_company)
dim(hotels_clean)
```

```{r}
names(hotels_clean)
```
## 3c: Find records that make no sense
```{r}
summary(hotels_clean[, c("adults", "children", "babies", "adr",
                         "stays_in_weekend_nights", "stays_in_week_nights",
                         "lead_time")])

sum(hotels_clean$adults + hotels_clean$children + hotels_clean$babies == 0)
sum(hotels_clean$stays_in_weekend_nights + hotels_clean$stays_in_week_nights == 0)
sum(hotels_clean$adr < 0)
```
What each part does:   **summary(...)** gives the minimum, quartiles, mean and maximum for seven numeric columns. adr is the average daily rate, the price per night.
**The first sum()** counts bookings where adults, children and babies add up to zero: a reservation for nobody.
**The second sum()** counts bookings with zero nights in total.
**The third sum()** counts bookings with a negative room rate.
Each sum() works because R treats TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0, so adding up a true/false test counts how many rows passed it.

```{r}
# 1. The negative price and any very high price
hotels_clean[hotels_clean$adr < 0 | hotels_clean$adr > 1000,
             c("hotel", "is_canceled", "adults", "adr",
               "deposit_type", "market_segment")]

# 2. Bookings with many babies or many adults
hotels_clean[hotels_clean$babies >= 9 | hotels_clean$adults >= 20,
             c("hotel", "is_canceled", "adults", "children", "babies",
               "adr", "market_segment")]

# 3. What happened to the zero-night bookings
table(hotels_clean$is_canceled[hotels_clean$stays_in_weekend_nights +
                               hotels_clean$stays_in_week_nights == 0])
```


| Finding           | Rows | Decision | Reason                                   |
|-------------------|------|----------|------------------------------------------|
| Negative price    | 1    | Remove   | Impossible                               |
| Price of 5,400    | 1    | Remove   | Isolated, implausible, distorts scaling  |
| Zero guests       | 180  | Remove   | Not a booking for anyone                 |
| 20 or more adults | 12   | Remove   | Zero-price placeholder entries           |
| 9 or more babies  | 2    | Remove   | Evident entry errors                     |
| Zero nights       | 715  | Keep     | Completed records, likely daytime use    |


That removes 196 rows, about 0.16% of the data. 


```{r}
drop <- hotels_clean$adr < 0 |
        hotels_clean$adr > 1000 |
        (hotels_clean$adults + hotels_clean$children + hotels_clean$babies) == 0 |
        hotels_clean$adults >= 20 |
        hotels_clean$babies >= 9

sum(drop)
hotels_clean <- hotels_clean[!drop, ]
dim(hotels_clean)
```
## Step 4a: Take stock of the text columns 
```{r}
text_cols <- sapply(hotels_clean, is.character)
sapply(hotels_clean[text_cols], function(x) length(unique(x)))
```
**What each line does**
**Line 1** tests every column and marks TRUE for the ones stored as text. sapply() applies a function to each column in turn.
**Line 2** takes only the text columns and, for each one, counts its distinct values. The function(x) length(unique(x)) part is a small function written on the spot: for a column x, count the unique values.

## Step 4b: Choose the predictors

```{r}
table(hotels_clean$market_segment, hotels_clean$distribution_channel)
```
### Proposed removals (5 columns)

| Column                      | Reason to remove                                                        |
|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `country`                   | 178 levels; would create about 178 dummy columns. Nationality may not be confirmed until check-in. |
| `distribution_channel`      | Overlaps with `market_segment`; adds columns without adding information |
| `arrival_date_year`         | Future years are not in the data; only reflects three past years        |
| `arrival_date_week_number`  | Duplicates the seasonal information in the arrival month                |
| `arrival_date_day_of_month` | No clear reason for day of month to affect cancellation                 |


### Predictors kept (22 columns)

| #  | Column                           | Type     | What it holds                                         |
|----|----------------------------------|----------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| 1  | `hotel`                          | Category | Resort Hotel or City Hotel                            |
| 2  | `arrival_date_month`             | Category | Month of arrival                                      |
| 3  | `meal`                           | Category | Meal package booked                                   |
| 4  | `market_segment`                 | Category | How the booking was sourced                           |
| 5  | `reserved_room_type`             | Category | Code of the room type reserved                        |
| 6  | `deposit_type`                   | Category | No Deposit, Non Refund or Refundable                  |
| 7  | `customer_type`                  | Category | Type of booking, such as transient, contract or group |
| 8  | `lead_time`                      | Number   | Days between booking and arrival                      |
| 9  | `stays_in_weekend_nights`        | Number   | Weekend nights booked                                 |
| 10 | `stays_in_week_nights`           | Number   | Week nights booked                                    |
| 11 | `adults`                         | Number   | Number of adults                                      |
| 12 | `children`                       | Number   | Number of children                                    |
| 13 | `babies`                         | Number   | Number of babies                                      |
| 14 | `is_repeated_guest`              | 0/1      | 1 if the guest has stayed before                      |
| 15 | `previous_cancellations`         | Number   | Earlier bookings this guest cancelled                 |
| 16 | `previous_bookings_not_canceled` | Number   | Earlier bookings this guest did not cancel            |
| 17 | `days_in_waiting_list`           | Number   | Days on the waiting list before confirmation          |
| 18 | `adr`                            | Number   | Average daily rate, in euros                          |
| 19 | `required_car_parking_spaces`    | Number   | Parking spaces requested                              |
| 20 | `total_of_special_requests`      | Number   | Number of special requests                            |
| 21 | `used_agent`                     | 0/1      | 1 if booked through a travel agent (created in Step 3b) |
| 22 | `used_company`                   | 0/1      | 1 if booked through a company (created in Step 3b)    |

Target: `is_canceled` (1 = the guest did not stay, 0 = the guest stayed).


## Step 4b: Remove the 5 columns
Check
```{r}
table(hotels_clean$market_segment, hotels_clean$distribution_channel)
```
Remove
```{r}
hotels_model <- subset(hotels_clean, select = -c(country, distribution_channel,
                                                 arrival_date_year,
                                                 arrival_date_week_number,
                                                 arrival_date_day_of_month))
dim(hotels_model)
names(hotels_model)
```
**What each line does**

**subset(..., select = -c(...))** keeps every column except the five listed after the minus sign.

**hotels_model** is a new object for modeling. hotels_clean still holds all 28 columns, so restoring one later is a single edit.

**dim()** reports the size.

**names()** lists the remaining columns so you can confirm the right ones are gone.

## Step 4c: Tell R which columns are categories

**The problem** R currently stores seven category columns as plain text, and the target as the numbers 0 and 1. The models need to know these are categories. R’s name for a category column is a factor.

```{r}
cat_cols <- c("hotel", "arrival_date_month", "meal", "market_segment",
              "reserved_room_type", "deposit_type", "customer_type")

hotels_model[cat_cols] <- lapply(hotels_model[cat_cols], factor)

hotels_model$arrival_date_month <- factor(hotels_model$arrival_date_month,
                                          levels = month.name)

hotels_model$is_canceled <- factor(hotels_clean$is_canceled,
                                   levels = c(0, 1),
                                   labels = c("Stayed", "Canceled"))

str(hotels_model)
table(hotels_model$is_canceled)
```
**What each part does**

**cat_cols** is a list of the seven category column names.

**lapply(..., factor) ** converts each of those seven columns to a factor in one step.

**The month line** puts the months in calendar order. Without it, R sorts them alphabetically, starting with April. month.name is R’s built-in list of January to December.

**The target line "is_cancelled"** converts 0 and 1 into the labels “Stayed” and “Canceled,” so confusion matrices will be readable without a key. “Canceled” here includes no-shows, as we defined it.

### The benchmark after cleaning
75,008 of 119,194 is 62.9%, so the naive rule is still 63%. Removing 196 rows did not shift the balance.

## Step 5: Split the data

### Why split into three sets

| Set        | Share | Used for                                          |
|------------|-------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Training   | 60%   | The models learn from these bookings              |
| Validation | 20%   | Tuning, for example choosing the best k for k-NN  |
| Test       | 20%   | The final comparison of the two models, used once |


## Step 5a: Split Data Code

```{r}
set.seed(123)
n <- nrow(hotels_model)
idx <- sample(n)

n_train <- round(0.6 * n)
n_valid <- round(0.2 * n)

train <- hotels_model[idx[1:n_train], ]
valid <- hotels_model[idx[(n_train + 1):(n_train + n_valid)], ]
test  <- hotels_model[idx[(n_train + n_valid + 1):n], ]

nrow(train); nrow(valid); nrow(test)
round(prop.table(table(train$is_canceled)), 3)
round(prop.table(table(valid$is_canceled)), 3)
round(prop.table(table(test$is_canceled)), 3)
```

## Step 6a: Turn categories into numbers
```{r}
## Step 6a: Turn categories into 0/1 columns
library(class)

x_train <- model.matrix(is_canceled ~ ., data = train)[, -1]
x_valid <- model.matrix(is_canceled ~ ., data = valid)[, -1]
x_test  <- model.matrix(is_canceled ~ ., data = test)[, -1]

y_train <- train$is_canceled
y_valid <- valid$is_canceled
y_test  <- test$is_canceled

dim(x_train)
```

## Step 6b: Put every column on the same scale
```{r}
## Step 6b: Scale using training means and standard deviations
means <- apply(x_train, 2, mean)
sds   <- apply(x_train, 2, sd)

keep <- sds > 0   # drop any column with no variation in training

x_train_s <- scale(x_train[, keep], center = means[keep], scale = sds[keep])
x_valid_s <- scale(x_valid[, keep], center = means[keep], scale = sds[keep])
x_test_s  <- scale(x_test[, keep],  center = means[keep], scale = sds[keep])

sum(!keep)
dim(x_train_s)
round(mean(x_train_s[, "lead_time"]), 2); round(sd(x_train_s[, "lead_time"]), 2)
```

## Step 6c: First run, one k

```{r}
## Step 6c: First k-NN run (k = 5), timed
set.seed(123)
timing <- system.time(
  pred_5 <- knn(train = x_train_s, test = x_valid_s, cl = y_train, k = 5)
)
timing["elapsed"]

table(Predicted = pred_5, Actual = y_valid)
mean(pred_5 == y_valid)
```
**Result (k = 5):** Accuracy was 80.3%, well above the 63% benchmark of always predicting "Stayed." The model caught 5,937 of 8,803 cancellations (67%), missed 2,866, and raised 1,828 false alarms. The run took about one minute, so testing several values of k is practical.

## Step 6d: Compare several values of k

```{r}
## Step 6d: Try several k values on the validation set
k_values <- c(1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 21)
results <- data.frame(k = k_values, accuracy = NA, caught = NA)

set.seed(123)
for (i in seq_along(k_values)) {
  pred <- knn(train = x_train_s, test = x_valid_s, cl = y_train, k = k_values[i])
  results$accuracy[i] <- mean(pred == y_valid)
  results$caught[i]   <- mean(pred[y_valid == "Canceled"] == "Canceled")
  cat("Finished k =", k_values[i], "\n")
}

results$accuracy <- round(results$accuracy, 3)
results$caught   <- round(results$caught, 3)
results
```
**Choosing k:** Accuracy was nearly flat (79.7%–80.5%), but the share of cancellations caught fell as k increased. We chose k = 3: it had the highest validation accuracy (80.5%) and caught 70% of cancellations, without the instability of k = 1.

## Step 6e: Final test, run once

```{r}
## Step 6e: Final k-NN evaluation on the test set (k = 3)
set.seed(123)
pred_test <- knn(train = x_train_s, test = x_test_s, cl = y_train, k = 3)

table(Predicted = pred_test, Actual = y_test)

accuracy <- mean(pred_test == y_test)
caught   <- mean(pred_test[y_test == "Canceled"] == "Canceled")
precision <- mean(y_test[pred_test == "Canceled"] == "Canceled")

round(c(accuracy = accuracy, caught = caught, precision = precision), 3)
```

**Test results (k = 3):** On the test set, k-NN reached 80.1% accuracy, compared with the 62.6% benchmark of always predicting "Stayed." It caught 69.4% of cancellations, and 75.6% of the bookings it flagged as canceled did cancel. These results closely match validation (80.5% accuracy, 70.0% caught), showing the model performs consistently on unseen bookings.
